title: The Philippines needs to turn fast growth into productive growth
gist: The Philippines has grown ~5% a year for 25 years, but over 90% of growth since 2010 came from capital accumulation with under 10% from productivity; electronics (54% of exports), IT-BPM, demographics, remittances and renewables are paths to productive growth, amid heavy US/China trade exposure and energy import dependence.

insights.claim: The Philippines has averaged 5% annual GDP growth over 25 years, two points above the global average, tripling its economy to 12.8% of ASEAN output.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Durable EM growth story, but quality of growth matters for long-run returns.
insights.locator: With an average annual GDP growth rate

insights.claim: Per the World Bank, over 90% of Philippine growth since 2010 came from capital accumulation, total factor productivity contributed under 10% and human capital was insignificant, risking the middle-income trap.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Capital-driven growth tends to decelerate; productivity reforms are the key upside catalyst.
insights.quote: it has been much better at generating growth than at generating productivity gains

insights.claim: Three-quarters of new Philippine jobs are in less productive non-tradable sectors, and about 16 million informal workers make up nearly one-third of employment.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Labour-market structure caps wage and productivity gains.

insights.claim: Logistics costs are roughly 27% of Philippine firm revenues, and high electricity prices tied to aging infrastructure and limited generation are a serious obstacle to industrialization.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Infrastructure, logistics and power-generation investment address the largest cost bottlenecks.

insights.claim: The World Bank estimates reforms in human capital, connectivity, competition and private investment could lift long-term growth by 1.4 points, create 5.1 million high-paying jobs by 2040 and raise real wages by nearly 13%.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Quantified upside if reforms occur — watch reform implementation as a re-rating trigger.

insights.claim: In 2025 the US took about 16% of Philippine exports while China accounted for nearly 22% of total trade and over 28.4% of imports; more than 75% of trade is concentrated in the US and East Asia.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: High sensitivity to US tariffs and Chinese supply chains; the author urges diversification including the EU.

insights.claim: Electronics generated $45.9 billion, or 54.3% of Philippine exports, in 2025, making the sector highly exposed to tariffs, export controls and tech restrictions.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Philippine export earnings hinge on the semiconductor cycle and US trade policy.
insights.locator: The exposure is particularly acute in electronics

insights.claim: 'China plus one' supply-chain diversification offers the Philippines an opening to attract semiconductor, electronics and advanced manufacturing investment and move from assembly and testing toward advanced packaging, chip design and R&D.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Potential FDI destination for chip back-end and packaging, competing with Vietnam and Malaysia.

insights.claim: The Philippines competes with Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia for diversified investment and must fix infrastructure, energy costs, logistics, skills and regulatory predictability.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Relative ASEAN FDI competitiveness hinges on these structural cost factors.
insights.locator: More than 75 percent of the country’s trade

insights.claim: Typhoons impose annual losses of about 1.2% of GDP and climate change could cut Philippine GDP by up to 13.6% by 2040 without action.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Material physical-climate risk for Philippine assets and sovereign credit.

insights.claim: The Philippines imports almost all its oil and about 80% of its coal; energy imports cost nearly $17 billion, or 17% of the total import bill, in 2025.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Oil price shocks hit the Philippine current account and peso hard.

insights.claim: The Philippines has large geothermal, solar, hydropower and offshore wind resources, including an estimated 894 GW of technical wind potential.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Renewables build-out is an investable theme with energy-security and fiscal benefits.

insights.claim: The Philippine IT-BPM industry generated over $40 billion in revenue and employed about 1.9 million workers in 2025; AI threatens some jobs but could move the industry into higher-value analytics, finance, health and cybersecurity services.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: AI is a key disruption risk for BPO outsourcing — watch Philippine BPO employment and revenue mix.

insights.claim: With nearly 117 million people, 55% under 30 and only 6% over 65, the Philippines has a demographic advantage as East Asia ages.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Long-run labour supply advantage supports consumption and services growth.

insights.claim: About 11 million Filipinos abroad sent nearly $40 billion in remittances in 2025, over 8% of GDP; better investment vehicles could channel this into domestic investment.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Remittances stabilise the current account; diaspora investment products are a potential growth niche.

insights.claim: At the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Manila should push supply-chain diversification in semiconductors and advanced services, partnerships for digital skills and AI readiness, and private capital for renewables and infrastructure.
insights.speaker: bpiasecki
insights.so_what: Watch Bangkok meetings for Philippine partnership and financing announcements.
